region_chill_delivered_provenance.mid_so: Chilling hours (hours near 35 to 45 degrees F during winter dormancy, Utah model) are banked across the whole Mid-South belt, but with a real intra-state gradient rather than a single flat figure. The University of Arkansas reports average accumulated chilling hours by March 1 at four stations: the northern Ozark upland (Fayetteville, zone 7) 1,024, the western station (Clarksville) 1,081, the northeastern Delta (Wynne) 1,069, and the southwestern warm edge (Hope, zone 8) 901. The cooler upland north and the delta bank on the order of 1,000 to 1,300 hours (zone 7); the warmer lowland south runs from Hope's roughly 900 hours up to about 1,100 (zone 8). Every zone clears the chilling requirement of the standard tree-fruit variety set (the highest canonical apple variety, McIntosh, needs about 900), though the southwestern warm edge clears it by the slimmest margin, so growers there should favor lower-chill varieties. Chill is a non-factor for blackberry (the belt's signature crop), which fruits many times over its requirement everywhere. Source: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension, Chilling Hour Reports (Utah model, 1990 to 2000 baseline). Verified 2026-07-20.
